summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for crash_2, grouped by the characteristic each names.

mechanisms.description: Patients with hyperfibrinolysis on point-of-care viscoelastic testing will derive greater mortality and transfusion-sparing benefit from targeted TXA because antifibrinolysis directly arrests pathologic clot breakdown and limits ongoing hemorrhage compared with treating unselected patients.

Shorter time from injury to TXA administration will increase benefit because early antifibrinolysis prevents progression of trauma-induced coagulopathy and irreversible hemorrhagic shock, whereas delayed treatment may fail to stabilize bleeding and could shift the balance toward thrombotic risk.

Marked hypotension on arrival will increase the relative benefit of TXA because severe hypoperfusion promotes fibrinolytic activation and clot instability that antifibrinolytics can counteract to reduce continued bleeding.

Persistent tachycardia indicative of ongoing hemorrhagic shock will modify benefit toward greater efficacy of TXA because sustained sympathetic-driven hypoperfusion amplifies consumptive coagulopathy with hyperfibrinolysis that antifibrinolysis can mitigate.

Severely low hemoglobin at presentation will blunt the relative benefit of TXA because profound blood loss necessitating transfusion limits the capacity of antifibrinolytic therapy alone to restore effective intravascular clotting and oxygen delivery.

Thrombocytopenia at baseline will reduce TXA effectiveness because inadequate platelet mass impairs primary haemostasis and preventing fibrin breakdown cannot compensate for failure of platelet plug formation.

A markedly elevated INR on admission will attenuate benefit from TXA because deficiencies in clotting factor–dependent fibrin generation limit formation of stable clots that antifibrinolytics act to preserve.

High base deficit indicating severe metabolic acidosis will reduce TXA efficacy because acidemia impairs enzymatic coagulation and fibrin formation, limiting the ability of antifibrinolytics to restore haemostatic competence.

Large intracranial hemorrhage on initial CT may alter the net effect of TXA because antifibrinolysis can reduce hematoma expansion but may also increase risk of ischemic complications in injured cerebral tissue predisposed to thrombotic occlusion.

Penetrating injuries will tend to show greater transfusion- and bleeding-control benefit from TXA because focal vascular disruption often produces high local fibrinolytic activity that antifibrinolytics can stabilize more effectively than diffuse blunt microvascular bleeding.

Patients on pre-injury anticoagulants will have attenuated benefit and potential harm from TXA because impaired thrombin generation or direct anticoagulant effects limit fibrin formation so antifibrinolytics cannot fully correct coagulopathy and may raise thrombotic risk as anticoagulant levels fall.

Pre-injury antiplatelet agent use will lessen the haemostatic benefit of TXA because platelet dysfunction undermines primary haemostasis and preventing fibrin breakdown cannot substitute for defective platelet plug formation.

Chronic liver disease at baseline will unpredictably modify TXA effects because combined reductions in pro- and anticoagulant factors and altered fibrinolytic regulators can make antifibrinolysis less effective for bleeding control and more likely to provoke thrombosis in some patients.

A history of prior venous thromboembolism will increase the likelihood of thrombotic harm from nonselective TXA because baseline prothrombotic tendency may be exacerbated by systemic inhibition of fibrinolysis, raising risk of recurrent occlusion.

Need for massive transfusion on arrival will predict greater benefit from targeted TXA because massive hemorrhage commonly induces hyperfibrinolysis and antifibrinolytic therapy can reduce ongoing clot breakdown and subsequent transfusion needs.
